lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, how does a comic show time passing? (In panels, one moment in each, read in order.) Today: animation, pictures that move.
Animation is a series of still pictures shown fast; the eye and brain join them into movement. Toys of the 1800s showed this: the thaumatrope (1825), the zoetrope (1834) and the flip-book.
Films show 24 frames a second. Animators often draw on twos: each drawing is shown for 2 frames, so 12 drawings make a second of film.
Timing is how many frames a movement takes: more frames, a slower movement. Spacing is how far it moves between frames. Here the spacing is even, so the ball moves like a robot.

Worked example: a real ball is slow at the top of its bounce and fast at the bottom. So the drawings bunch together at the top and spread out lower down: slow in and slow out. It squashes as it lands.
Stop-motion moves models a tiny bit between photos. Lotte Reiniger (1899-1981) cut paper silhouettes for The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926), the oldest animated feature film that survives.
Animators' rules of thumb: squash and stretch; anticipation, a small move back before a big one; arcs; and follow-through, as hair and tails keep moving after a stop.
Try it in the world: draw a bouncing ball on 12 sticky notes and flip them. Or make a Short in the game: SHORTS, then MAKE A SHORT. Next: sculpture and installation.

exercises.prompt: Film shows 24 frames a second. How many frames are in 3 seconds?
exercises.hint: Multiply the frames a second by the seconds.

choices: spins pictures so they seem to move
exercises.hint: Think of the toys from the 1800s.
exercises.explain: A zoetrope spins a strip of drawings past slits, so they seem to move.

exercises.prompt: Using more frames for the same movement makes it look slower.
exercises.explain: True: at 24 frames a second, more frames take longer to show, so the movement is slower.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: how far it moves each frame
a small move before a big one
how many frames a move takes
exercises.hint: Think of a ball's bounce and a jump.
exercises.explain: Timing is frames, spacing is distance each frame, squash is flattening and anticipation comes before a move.

exercises.prompt: Is this ball's spacing even, or slow in and slow out?
choices: even: the same gap every frame
exercises.hint: Compare the gaps at the top with the gaps lower down.
exercises.explain: Every gap is the same size, so it is even spacing: the ball would move like a robot.

exercises.prompt: An animator draws on twos at 24 frames a second. How many drawings are in 5 seconds?
exercises.hint: On twos, how many drawings make one second?

exercises.prompt: Where does this ball move slowest?
choices: at the top of the bounce
in the middle of the fall
exercises.hint: Where are the drawings closest together?
exercises.explain: The drawings bunch together at the top, so it moves least between frames there: slow in and slow out.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to make a stop-motion film.
items: build the models and the set
move a model a tiny bit
exercises.hint: Plan, build, then move and shoot.
exercises.explain: Plan, build, then move and photograph again and again, and finally play the photos fast.

items: paper cut-outs moved under a camera
exercises.hint: Is it drawn, or is a real thing moved?
exercises.explain: Flip-books, drawings on twos and zoetrope strips are drawn; clay and paper cut-outs are moved and photographed.

exercises.prompt: The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926) is the oldest animated feature film that survives.
exercises.explain: True: Lotte Reiniger's film of 1926 is the oldest surviving animated feature.

exercises.prompt: A movement takes 36 frames at 24 frames a second. How many seconds is that?
exercises.hint: Divide the frames by the frames a second.

exercises.prompt: A 2-minute Short is drawn on twos at 24 frames a second. How many drawings is that?
exercises.hint: Find the seconds and the drawings a second first.
exercises.explain: 2 minutes = 120 seconds; on twos, 24 ÷ 2 = 12 drawings a second; 120 × 12 = 1,440 drawings.

exercises.prompt: A character jumps. Which shows anticipation?
choices: bending the knees before the jump
exercises.hint: Anticipation comes before the main move.
exercises.explain: Bending the knees first gets ready for the jump: anticipation. Hair moving after is follow-through.

exercises.prompt: Even spacing makes a bouncing ball look natural.
exercises.hint: Where does a real ball move slowly?
exercises.explain: False: a real ball slows at the top, so natural spacing bunches up there; even spacing looks robotic.

exercises.prompt: A ball's fall takes 6 frames. To make the fall last twice as long, how many frames should it take?
exercises.hint: Twice as long needs twice as many frames.

exercises.prompt: Match each rule of thumb to an example.
matches: a tail swinging after a stop
an arm swinging on a curve
a ball flattening on the floor
exercises.hint: Picture each movement, then find its rule.
exercises.explain: Flattening is squash, a crouch is anticipation, a swinging tail is follow-through and a curved swing is an arc.
